statement:
A machine has k identical GPUs, each with cap GiB of memory. There are n jobs to place on them; job i needs jobs[i] GiB of memory. A job must sit entirely on one GPU and cannot be split; a GPU can hold several jobs as long as their memory adds up to at most cap. An assignment is a list assign of length n, where assign[i] is the number of the GPU job i is on (0 to k - 1).

Input ranges: 0 <= n <= 14, 1 <= k <= 14, 1 <= jobs[i] <= 10**6, 1 <= cap <= 10**7, all integers. Inputs are guaranteed to be in range; no validation needed. When n = 0, the empty list [] is a valid assignment.

Node counting. The interviewer will count how many nodes your search visits: each call of the recursive function counts as one node, including the very first call and the call made once all jobs have been placed. Every function takes an optional dict stats and, before returning, writes the node count to stats["nodes"]. This number depends only on how the code searches, not on how fast the machine is, so below it is used instead of running time to compare the effect of pruning.

Part 1 — Find an assignment

def pack(jobs: list[int], k: int, cap: int, stats: dict | None = None) -> list[int] | None: ...

Return the lexicographically smallest valid assign (compare assign[0] first, then assign[1] on a tie, and so on); return None if there is no valid assignment. This part only needs to be correct; the interviewer tests it only on inputs with n <= 8.

jobs = [3, 5, 2, 4], k = 2, cap = 7  ->  [0, 1, 1, 0]    GPU 0 holds 3 + 4 = 7, GPU 1 holds 5 + 2 = 7
jobs = [3, 5, 2, 4], k = 3, cap = 5  ->  [0, 1, 0, 2]    3 + 2 = 5, 5, 4
jobs = [3, 5, 2, 4], k = 2, cap = 6  ->  None            total 14 > 2 × 6
jobs = [8],          k = 2, cap = 7  ->  None            a single job does not fit
jobs = [],           k = 3, cap = 1  ->  []

Part 2 — Pruning

Now n can be up to 14. Return any valid assignment (it no longer has to be the lexicographically smallest; the interviewer only checks that it is valid), or None if there is none.

def pack_fast(jobs: list[int], k: int, cap: int, stats: dict | None = None) -> list[int] | None: ...

The two inputs below each have 12 jobs and 4 GPUs. Counted with the Part 1 reference approach (jobs processed in input order, GPUs tried from the smallest number up, check that a job fits before placing it, stop at the first solution), the number of nodes visited is:

A: jobs = [6, 9, 13, 15, 8, 9, 10, 15, 3, 3, 23, 30], k = 4, cap = 36

   the Part 1 approach visits 66005 nodes

   infeasible: total 244 = 4 × 61, so every GPU must be exactly full; but the only jobs that fit alongside 40
   are 13, 13, 9, 9, 7, 6, and no subset of them adds up to the 21 that 40's GPU still needs
   the Part 1 approach visits 350105 nodes

Requirements: on both A and B, visit at most one percent of the nodes above; inputs with n = 14, including hard ones where the job sizes are all similar and they only just fail to fit, should finish in about a second. Explain why each pruning never misses a solution, and why it saves so many nodes.

Part 3 — Keep the busiest GPU as empty as possible

cap is no longer given. The peak of an assignment is the largest memory usage over all GPUs. Find an assignment with the smallest peak.

def min_peak(jobs: list[int], k: int, stats: dict | None = None) -> tuple[int, list[int]]: ...
# returns (smallest possible peak, one assignment that reaches it); any such assignment is accepted

When n = 0, return (0, []). With n = 14 it should finish in about a second; reuse the Part 2 code as much as you can.

jobs = [3, 5, 2, 4],    k = 3  ->  peak 5    {5}, {3, 2}, {4}
A, k = 4                       ->  peak 36
B, k = 4                       ->  peak 62   total / 4 is 61, but Part 2 showed that 61 does not fit
jobs = [],              k = 2  ->  peak 0
solution:
Two things are worth confirming before you start. First, can a job be split across two GPUs? No; otherwise the problem reduces to simple division. Second, are the GPUs identical? Yes. This decides whether the most effective pruning in Part 2 can be used at all; once the problem changes to "each GPU has a different amount of memory", that pruning has to change with it.

Part 1

Idea. Decide where each job goes, one job at a time. For job i, try every GPU that can still hold it, in increasing order of number: place it there and recurse on job i + 1; if the rest fails, take it back off (undo) and try the next GPU. If every GPU has been tried without success, report failure to the level above.

Invariant. When place(i) is called, loads[g] is exactly the total memory of the jobs among 0..i-1 placed on GPU g, and every loads[g] is at most cap. The undo line loads[g] -= jobs[i] is there so that the invariant still holds on returning to the level above.

Why the result is the lexicographically smallest assignment. The search visits partial assignments in lexicographic order: it first fixes the smallest possible value of assign[0], under that the smallest possible value of assign[1], and so on. A branch cut by "does not fit" already has a GPU over cap, and memory only grows as more jobs are added, so there is no valid assignment below such a branch. Therefore the first complete assignment the search reaches is the lexicographically smallest valid one.

Complexity. Level d of the search tree has at most kd nodes and each node tries k GPUs, so the worst case is O(kn+1) time; space is the recursion depth plus two arrays, O(n+k). That is fine for n <= 8, but with n = 14, k = 4 it is 414≈2.7×108, which is too slow.

def pack(jobs, k, cap, stats=None):
    n = len(jobs)
    loads = [0] * k           # loads[g]: memory used on GPU g by jobs 0..i-1
    assign = [0] * n
    nodes = 0

    def place(i):
        nonlocal nodes
        nodes += 1
        if i == n:
            return True
        for g in range(k):    # smaller GPU numbers first, so the first full assignment is the smallest one
            if loads[g] + jobs[i] <= cap:
                loads[g] += jobs[i]
                assign[i] = g
                if place(i + 1):
                    return True
                loads[g] -= jobs[i]          # undo before trying the next GPU
        return False

    found = place(0)
    if stats is not None:
        stats["nodes"] = nodes
    return assign if found else None

Part 2

Part 1 is slow not because each node does a lot of work, but because it spends most of its time in subtrees that are doomed to fail. The two prunings each attack one of the two causes.

Pruning 1: place the large jobs first. Sort the jobs by memory in decreasing order before searching. Large jobs have the fewest GPUs they can go to; placing them first exposes conflicts close to the root, where a single failure cuts away a whole large subtree. Searching in input order, the largest job in B, 40, is 11th in line, so every arrangement of the first 10 jobs is enumerated first, and each one only discovers at level 11 that 40 does not fit. Sorting changes only the order of the search, not what is searched, so no solution is missed. The idea is usually called "most constrained variable first" (fail-first).

Pruning 2: symmetry between GPUs. The GPUs are identical. If two GPUs currently have the same load, then whichever of them the current job goes into, the two subtrees below are mirror images: swapping the numbers of the two GPUs turns every assignment in one subtree into an assignment in the other, and both are valid. So only one GPU per load value needs to be tried. The most common case is empty GPUs: all empty GPUs are equivalent, so try just one. Without this rule the first job has k equivalent choices, the second job another k - 1, and so on, and the whole tree is pointlessly duplicated many times over.

Correctness. Suppose a valid assignment puts job i on GPU g2, while another GPU g1 had the same load as g2 just before job i was placed. Swap g1 and g2 for job i and every job after it: the two GPUs' final loads are exactly exchanged, both still at most cap, and the part before job i is unchanged. So skipping g2 cannot lose the conclusion "a solution exists".

In addition, before searching do two O(n) checks: the total must not exceed k * cap, and the largest job must not exceed cap. If either fails, return None immediately and record 0 nodes.

Effect. The table below gives the nodes each version visits on A and B from the statement (each entry is asserted in the verification code):

Version A (feasible) B (infeasible)
Part 1 as is 66005 350105
Symmetry pruning only 15491 13356
Decreasing size only 13 1577
Both 13 16

After sorting, A succeeds on the first dive: 13 = n + 1 nodes, with no backtracking at all. For B, proving infeasibility, neither pruning is enough on its own; together they bring it down to 16 nodes. After sorting, the first four jobs 40, 31, 31, 31 exceed 61 in any pair, so each takes its own GPU, and the symmetry pruning leaves only one way to do that; next, 30 can only go with one of the 31s, and 24 only into one of the remaining 31s, and within a few steps the search hits a dead end.

How much it saves depends on the input. On the random inputs in the verification code (n from 9 to 11, k 3 or 4, job sizes 5 to 40), for infeasible inputs with cap one less than the optimal peak, the median node count shrinks by a few hundred times, and no input gets worse; for feasible inputs with cap exactly equal to the optimal peak, the median shrinks only a few times, and some inputs actually take more nodes, because the original order happened to run into a solution very early. Most of the benefit of pruning comes when the whole tree must be searched: proving infeasibility or, as in Part 3, proving that no better solution exists.

Complexity. The worst case is still exponential: with k = 2 this is the partition problem, which is NP-complete, so do not expect a polynomial algorithm. An upper bound you can give: with the symmetry pruning, distinct nodes at level d correspond to distinct ways of splitting the first d jobs into at most k unlabeled groups (where two paths first diverge, the current job went into two GPUs with different loads, and hence different sets of jobs), so level d has at most ∑j≤k​S(d,j) nodes, where S are the Stirling numbers of the second kind; that is far less than kd, and the cap constraint cuts most of it away. Each node does O(k) work, and space is O(n+k).

def pack_fast(jobs, k, cap, stats=None, sort_desc=True, skip_equal=True):
    """Any valid assignment or None. The two switches exist only so that the checks can measure each pruning."""
    n = len(jobs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -jobs[i]) if sort_desc else list(range(n))
    loads = [0] * k
    assign = [0] * n
    nodes = 0

    def place(pos):
        nonlocal nodes
        nodes += 1
        if pos == n:
            return True
        i = order[pos]                       # the pos-th largest job
        tried = set()                        # loads already tried for this job at this node
        for g in range(k):
            if loads[g] + jobs[i] > cap:
                continue
            if skip_equal:
                if loads[g] in tried:        # NOTE: same load as a GPU tried before, so the subtree is a mirror image
                    continue
                tried.add(loads[g])
            loads[g] += jobs[i]
            assign[i] = g
            if place(pos + 1):
                return True
            loads[g] -= jobs[i]
        return False

    found = sum(jobs) <= k * cap and max(jobs, default=0) <= cap and place(0)
    if stats is not None:
        stats["nodes"] = nodes
    return assign if found else None

Part 3

This is an optimization problem. Search the same tree, but instead of stopping at the first solution, keep track of the best solution so far (the incumbent) while searching, and use it to prune. This approach is called branch and bound.

  1. Get a decent solution greedily first. Take the jobs from largest to smallest and put each on the currently least loaded GPU (this greedy is called LPT, longest processing time first). Its peak is the initial best.
  2. Compute a lower bound. The peak of any assignment is at least the largest job, and at least ⌈total/k⌉. Call the larger of the two lower. If the greedy already reaches lower, return right away without searching.
  3. Prune during the search. Keep the sorting and symmetry pruning from Part 2. After placing a job, if that GPU's load is already >= best, every assignment below this branch has a peak >= best and cannot be strictly better, so skip it. This amounts to running the Part 2 search with cap = best - 1 at every moment, and as best keeps shrinking, the pruning gets more and more aggressive.
  4. Update at a leaf. Reaching a leaf means every step on the way stayed < best, so this is a strictly better solution; record it. As soon as best == lower, nothing can do better, so end the whole search immediately.

Correctness. Every pruned branch has a peak >= best and cannot be a strictly better solution; the argument for the symmetry pruning is the same as in Part 2 (swapping the numbers of two GPUs does not change the peak). So when the search ends, best is the smallest peak.

Effect. Without the "prune at >= best" rule (keeping everything else, including the greedy initial value and stopping at the lower bound), A takes 700662 nodes and B 624928; with it, 13 and 16 respectively. The verification code also has an input where the greedy gives 69, the lower bound is 61 and the optimum is 62: branch and bound visits 4424 nodes, versus 2412066 without the rule.

Complexity. The worst case is likewise exponential. At every node the search reaches, every GPU's load is below the greedy peak, so the node count is at most that of the Part 2 search with cap = greedy peak - 1, run over the whole tree without stopping at a solution. Sorting is O(nlogn), the greedy O(nk), each node O(k), and space O(n+k). The verification code picks out the randomly generated n = 14 inputs that take the most nodes and prints their running times.

def min_peak(jobs, k, stats=None, use_bound=True):
    """(smallest peak, an assignment reaching it). use_bound=False only exists so the checks can measure the bound."""
    n = len(jobs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -jobs[i])
    loads = [0] * k
    assign = [0] * n
    for i in order:                          # greedy LPT: largest job onto the least loaded GPU
        g = loads.index(min(loads))
        loads[g] += jobs[i]
        assign[i] = g
    best, best_assign = max(loads), assign[:]
    lower = max(max(jobs, default=0), -(-sum(jobs) // k))
    loads = [0] * k
    nodes = 0

    def place(pos, peak):
        nonlocal best, best_assign, nodes
        nodes += 1
        if pos == n:
            if peak < best:                  # always true here: every step on the way stayed below best
                best, best_assign = peak, assign[:]
            return
        i = order[pos]
        tried = set()
        for g in range(k):
            new = loads[g] + jobs[i]
            if loads[g] in tried or (use_bound and new >= best):     # NOTE: >= because only a strictly better plan helps
                continue
            tried.add(loads[g])
            loads[g] = new
            assign[i] = g
            place(pos + 1, max(peak, new))
            loads[g] = new - jobs[i]
            if best == lower:                # nothing can beat the lower bound: unwind the whole search
                return

    if best > lower:
        place(0, 0)
    if stats is not None:
        stats["nodes"] = nodes               # search nodes only; the greedy pass is not counted
    return best, best_assign

Follow-up questions

  • Why not just use the greedy? LPT is not always optimal. Take [3, 3, 2, 2, 2], k = 2 from the statement: the greedy first separates the two 3s, then places the three 2s in turn, giving {3, 2, 2} and {3, 2} with peak 7, while the optimum is 6. Graham proved that LPT's peak is at most 34​−3k1​ times the optimum, and the verification code checks this bound on random inputs. The greedy is good as an initial value and a fallback; search only when you need the exact optimum.
  • Could you binary search on the peak, calling Part 2 each time? Yes: the answer lies in [lower, greedy peak]; binary search over it, using pack_fast each time to decide whether everything fits, with a logarithmic number of calls. The downside is that every "does not fit" answer has to search the whole tree, which is exactly the most expensive kind of search; branch and bound keeps tightening best within a single search, so nothing already searched is repeated. The verification code cross-checks the binary-search version against min_peak.
  • When does backtracking turn into dynamic programming? When the same state is reached again and again. After sorting, once the first pos jobs are placed, the remaining problem depends only on the multiset of GPU loads, not on which job is on which GPU. So you can keep the failed (pos, sorted loads) pairs in a set and return failure immediately when one comes up again; that is search with memoization, which is dynamic programming. Whether it helps depends on whether states repeat: with 14 jobs all of size 5, k = 4, cap = 19, the node count drops from 2035 to 61; when the job sizes are all different, load combinations almost never repeat, and memoization only costs memory. Another formulation is a DP over subsets of jobs: f[j][mask] is the smallest peak when placing the jobs in mask on j GPUs, enumerating the subset that goes on the last GPU, in O(k⋅3n) time. Its running time does not depend on luck, and the verification code uses it as an independent brute force.
  • If some jobs cannot share a GPU (for example, two jobs that both need exclusive use of some device), which prunings still hold? Placing large jobs first still holds, since it only changes the search order; jobs with many conflicts should also be placed early. The symmetry pruning has to be tightened: two GPUs with the same load but different jobs on them conflict differently with later jobs, so they are no longer mirror images. Only completely empty GPUs are still equivalent, so the only rule you can keep is "try just one empty GPU".
  • What happens if n grows a bit, say 16 jobs of similar size? It gets slow. The verification code has an input with 16 jobs, all between 1005 and 1049 in size, and k = 5; with cap one less than the optimal peak, pack_fast has to visit 3904649 nodes to prove infeasibility. You can add a "wasted space" pruning: if the space left on a GPU is smaller than the smallest job, that space can never be used; prune when the total waste exceeds k * cap - total. On this input the node count drops to 1043003, saving only about three quarters, and it is still exponential. At this scale the more realistic options are to switch to an integer programming solver, or to accept the greedy approximation.

import itertools
import random
import time

A = [6, 9, 13, 15, 8, 9, 10, 15, 3, 3, 23, 30]
B = [31, 7, 13, 6, 30, 9, 9, 13, 31, 24, 40, 31]
C = [19, 19, 27, 27, 17, 16, 32, 34, 36, 28, 17, 29]


def is_valid(jobs, k, cap, assign):
    if assign is None or len(assign) != len(jobs) or any(not 0 <= g < k for g in assign):
        return False
    loads = [0] * k
    for size, g in zip(jobs, assign):
        loads[g] += size
    return max(loads, default=0) <= cap


def peak_of(jobs, k, assign):
    loads = [0] * k
    for size, g in zip(jobs, assign):
        loads[g] += size
    return max(loads, default=0)


def run(fn, *args, **kw):
    stats = {}
    out = fn(*args, stats=stats, **kw)
    return out, stats["nodes"]


# ---- independent brute forces ----
def brute_first(jobs, k, cap):
    """itertools.product yields assignments in lexicographic order, so the first valid one is the smallest."""
    for assign in itertools.product(range(k), repeat=len(jobs)):
        if is_valid(jobs, k, cap, list(assign)):
            return list(assign)
    return None


def brute_peak(jobs, k):
    return min(peak_of(jobs, k, a) for a in itertools.product(range(k), repeat=len(jobs)))


def subset_dp_peak(jobs, k):
    """f[mask] after j rounds: smallest peak placing the jobs in mask on j GPUs. O(k * 3^n)."""
    n = len(jobs)
    total = [0] * (1 << n)
    for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
        low = mask & -mask
        total[mask] = total[mask ^ low] + jobs[low.bit_length() - 1]
    f = total[:]
    for _ in range(k - 1):
        g = f[:]
        for mask in range(1 << n):
            sub = mask
            while sub:
                cand = max(f[mask ^ sub], total[sub])
                if cand < g[mask]:
                    g[mask] = cand
                sub = (sub - 1) & mask
        f = g
    return f[(1 << n) - 1]

def lpt(jobs, k):
    loads = [0] * k
    for size in sorted(jobs, reverse=True):
        loads[loads.index(min(loads))] += size
    return max(loads, default=0)

    jobs = [rng.randint(1, rng.choice([2, 5, 12, 10 ** 6])) for _ in range(n)]

    cap = max(1, best + rng.choice([-3, -1, 0, 0, 1, 4]))
    want = brute_first(jobs, k, cap)
    assert pack(jobs, k, cap) == want, (jobs, k, cap)
    fast = pack_fast(jobs, k, cap)
    assert (fast is None) == (want is None) and (fast is None or is_valid(jobs, k, cap, fast)), (jobs, k, cap)
    p, assign = min_peak(jobs, k)
    assert p == best and peak_of(jobs, k, assign) == p and len(assign) == n, (jobs, k)
    saw_none += want is None
    saw_some += want is not None
    saw_lex_differs += fast is not None and fast != want
assert min(saw_none, saw_some, saw_lex_differs) >= 100, (saw_none, saw_some, saw_lex_differs)

def median(xs):

    return xs[len(xs) // 2]

# the Stirling-number bound on the nodes per level of the pruned search
def stirling_rows(n, k):
    S = [[0] * (k + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    S[0][0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for j in range(1, k + 1):
            S[i][j] = S[i - 1][j - 1] + j * S[i - 1][j]
    return [sum(row) for row in S]


assert sum(stirling_rows(12, 4)) == 934120 and sum(4 ** d for d in range(13)) == 22369621

    bound = sum(stirling_rows(n, k))

def full_tree_nodes(jobs, k, cap):
    """Nodes of the Part 2 tree (sorted order, one GPU per load value) when the search never stops early."""
    order = sorted(jobs, reverse=True)
    loads = [0] * k

    def count(pos):
        total = 1
        if pos < len(order):
            tried = set()
            for g in range(k):
                if loads[g] + order[pos] <= cap and loads[g] not in tried:
                    tried.add(loads[g])
                    loads[g] += order[pos]
                    total += count(pos + 1)
                    loads[g] -= order[pos]
        return total

    return count(0)

# ---- follow-ups ----
def min_peak_bisect(jobs, k):
    lo, hi = max(max(jobs, default=0), -(-sum(jobs) // k)), lpt(jobs, k)
    while lo < hi:                                   # invariant: the answer lies in [lo, hi]
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if pack_fast(jobs, k, mid) is not None:
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo


def pack_memo(jobs, k, cap, stats=None):
    """pack_fast plus a set of dead states (pos, sorted loads): backtracking that remembers is a DP."""
    n = len(jobs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -jobs[i])
    loads, assign, dead, nodes = [0] * k, [0] * n, set(), 0

    def place(pos):
        nonlocal nodes
        nodes += 1
        if pos == n:
            return True
        key = (pos, tuple(sorted(loads)))
        if key in dead:
            return False
        i, tried = order[pos], set()
        for g in range(k):
            if loads[g] + jobs[i] > cap or loads[g] in tried:
                continue
            tried.add(loads[g])
            loads[g] += jobs[i]
            assign[i] = g
            if place(pos + 1):
                return True
            loads[g] -= jobs[i]
        dead.add(key)
        return False

    found = sum(jobs) <= k * cap and max(jobs, default=0) <= cap and place(0)
    if stats is not None:
        stats["nodes"] = nodes
    return assign if found else None


def pack_waste(jobs, k, cap, stats=None):
    """pack_fast plus the wasted-space bound from the last follow-up."""
    n = len(jobs)
    order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: -jobs[i])
    loads, assign, nodes = [0] * k, [0] * n, 0
    smallest, allowed = min(jobs, default=0), k * cap - sum(jobs)

    def place(pos, waste):
        nonlocal nodes
        nodes += 1
        if pos == n:
            return True
        i, tried = order[pos], set()
        for g in range(k):
            new = loads[g] + jobs[i]
            if new > cap or loads[g] in tried:
                continue
            tried.add(loads[g])
            lost = cap - new if cap - new < smallest else 0      # no remaining job fits in what is left
            if waste + lost > allowed:
                continue
            loads[g] = new
            assign[i] = g
            if place(pos + 1, waste + lost):
                return True
            loads[g] = new - jobs[i]
        return False

    found = allowed >= 0 and max(jobs, default=0) <= cap and place(0, 0)
    if stats is not None:
        stats["nodes"] = nodes
    return assign if found else None


for _ in range(1500):
    n = rng.randint(0, 10)
    k = rng.randint(1, 4)
    jobs = [rng.randint(1, rng.choice([2, 3, 10, 40])) for _ in range(n)]
    cap = rng.randint(1, 45)
    want_none = pack_fast(jobs, k, cap) is None
    for fn in (pack_memo, pack_waste):
        out, nodes = run(fn, jobs, k, cap)
        assert (out is None) == want_none and (out is None or is_valid(jobs, k, cap, out)), (fn.__name__, jobs, k, cap)
        assert nodes <= run(pack_fast, jobs, k, cap)[1]
    if n:
        assert min_peak_bisect(jobs, k) == min_peak(jobs, k)[0]
